level
1 to 6.2, including 1b (default auto) - Decoder level written to the stream; x264 only warns, it clamps nothing
Tuning & Profile

The decoder level written into the stream header. Levels bound resolution, frame rate, bitrate and how many reference frames may be buffered, and hardware decoders advertise the highest level they implement.

x264 works out a suitable level on its own, so this is only worth setting when a target demands a specific one - Blu-ray at 4.1, or a device that refuses anything higher.

Be aware that x264 only warns when your other settings exceed the level you asked for; it does not reduce ref frames or anything else to fit. Getting a conformant stream means setting those yourself.

4.1|Blu-ray, and a very common hardware ceiling for 1080p.
5.1|4K delivery to modern decoders.
3.0|Older mobile devices at standard definition.
1b|The lowest level there is, for legacy handset profiles.
cabac
0 or 1 (default 1) - Entropy coder: 1 is CABAC, 0 the older CAVLC that only very limited decoders need
Tuning & Profile

H.264 has two entropy coders. CABAC is arithmetic coding and is worth something on the order of ten percent of the bitrate at the same quality; CAVLC is the variable-length coder the Baseline profile is limited to, and it is cheaper to decode.

There is no quality reason to turn CABAC off. The reasons are compatibility - a Baseline-only decoder cannot read it - and decode cost, since CABAC is inherently serial and is the first thing to give way on hardware that cannot keep up.

It is one of the tools any decode-cost tuning drops for exactly that reason. Leave it on for anything a current device will play.

1|The default; CABAC, and worth around ten percent of the bitrate.
0|CAVLC, for Baseline decoders and very weak playback hardware.
8x8dct
0 or 1 (default 1) - The High profile 8x8 transform; off drops the stream to Main profile and costs efficiency
Tuning & Profile

Allows the 8x8 integer transform alongside the 4x4 one, so flat and smoothly varying areas can be coded as one larger block instead of four small ones. It is a High profile tool and one of the larger single wins H.264 has over what came before it.

Turning it off restricts the encoder to 4x4 transforms and drops the stream to Main profile. That costs a few percent of the bitrate and softens large smooth areas, and the only reason to do it is a decoder that implements Main and nothing above.

It takes i8x8 out of the partition set with it, so a partitions list naming i8x8 will not get it while this is off.

1|The default; the 8x8 transform on, as every current decoder expects.
0|Main profile output, for a decoder that cannot do High.
deblock
alpha,beta each -6 to 6 (default 0,0) - Loop filter strength; negative keeps grain, positive hides blocking
Tuning & Profile

Offsets for the in-loop deblocking filter, which smooths the edges between coded blocks before the frame is used as a reference. The first number shifts the filter's strength and the second the threshold at which an edge is considered worth filtering.

Negative values filter less, so grain and fine texture survive the loop instead of being averaged away - at the cost of visible block edges if the bitrate is not there to support them. Positive values filter more, which hides blocking at low bitrates and costs detail.

Write the two numbers separated by a comma. x264's own documentation spells this alpha:beta, and a colon is what separates one parameter from the next in the string this grid builds - so a colon here splits the value in half and the row is refused. A single number sets both.

0,0|The default, neutral filtering.
-1,-1|A mild sharpening, common for detailed live action.
-3,-3|Strongly preserves grain; needs a generous bitrate or it blocks.
1,1|Smooths more, for low bitrate encodes where blocking shows.
psy
0 or 1 (default 1) - Master switch for the psychovisual optimisations; off raises PSNR and looks worse
Tuning & Profile

Turns x264's psychovisual optimisations on or off as a group - psy-rd, psy-trellis, and the small chroma quantiser bias that goes with them. On, the encoder prefers a block that keeps the same amount of visual energy as the source over one that measures closer to it; off, it takes the lowest measurable error every time.

Off is a benchmarking setting. It raises PSNR and SSIM, which is exactly why it is not something to ship: those metrics reward the smoothing psy exists to stop.

The chroma bias is worth knowing about because nothing else mentions it. With psy on, x264 applies a chroma-qp-offset of -2 of its own on top of whatever you set, so a stream encoded at the defaults reports -2 rather than 0; turning psy off removes it and the same stream reports 0.

None of this does anything below subme 6, which is where rate-distortion optimisation starts.

1|The default; psychovisual optimisations on.
0|Off, for PSNR and SSIM benchmarking only.
bframes
0-16 (default 3) - B-frames between I and P frames; more helps low-motion and animated sources, costs latency
Frames & Motion

The longest run of consecutive B-frames the encoder may insert. B-frames predict from both earlier and later frames, which makes them by far the cheapest frames to code, so allowing longer runs lets static and slow material spend its bits where something is actually happening.

Returns fall off past five or so on live action, and beyond about eight almost nothing is gained on any source. Animation and static footage benefit the most because long stretches genuinely do not change.

Every B-frame adds encoding latency and a frame of decode delay, which is why low-latency settings put this at 0.

3|The default, a sound balance for live action.
0|Baseline profile output and low-latency streaming.
8|Animation and mostly static footage, where long runs pay off.
16|The maximum; realistically no better than 8.
b-adapt
0-2 (default 1) - How B-frame placement is decided: 0 off, 1 fast, 2 optimal but slow with high bframes
Frames & Motion

Decides where in the sequence B-frames actually go, up to the limit bframes sets. 0 skips the decision and always uses the maximum run, which is fast and usually wasteful. 1 is a quick heuristic. 2 runs a proper search over the possibilities and picks the best arrangement.

Mode 2 is the one worth having on anything not being encoded in real time, but its cost grows with the bframes setting, so pairing b-adapt 2 with a large bframes value is where slow presets spend a lot of their time.

1|The default, a fast heuristic that is right most of the time.
2|Slower and better; the choice for offline encoding.
0|Fastest, always using the maximum run; for real-time only.
b-pyramid
none, strict or normal (default normal) - Whether B-frames may themselves be used as references
Frames & Motion

Normally B-frames are never referenced by anything, so they are disposable. B-pyramid allows some of them to act as references for other B-frames, which builds a hierarchy and improves compression noticeably on material with long B-frame runs.

normal is the default and allows the full arrangement. strict limits the structure to what the Blu-ray specification permits, which is what to use for disc authoring.

none disables it. That costs efficiency, and is only needed for decoders that cannot cope with referenced B-frames.

normal|The default; full hierarchical B-frames.
strict|The restricted form Blu-ray authoring requires.
none|No referenced B-frames, for limited decoders.
scenecut
0-100 (default 40) - How readily a shot change forces an I-frame; 0 leaves only the fixed keyframe interval
Frames & Motion

The threshold at which the lookahead decides a frame differs enough from the one before it to be worth coding as an I-frame rather than predicting from it. Higher values insert keyframes more readily, lower values less, and 0 turns adaptive keyframes off entirely.

An I-frame at a cut is close to free - there was nothing worth predicting from anyway - and it stops the first moment of each new shot looking soft, so the default is what you want for ordinary viewing.

0 is for when keyframe positions have to be predictable: segmented streaming, or a file that will be cut on a keyframe later. The cost is a visible smear at every cut that lands mid-GOP. The keyframe interval itself is set by the tab and is not one of these rows.

40|The default; adaptive keyframes at shot changes.
0|Fixed GOP only, for segmented streaming and keyframe-exact cutting.
60|Inserts keyframes more freely; faster seeking, slightly larger files.
25|More reluctant, saving bits on content that cuts constantly.
ref
1-16 (default 3) - Reference frames the motion search may use; more helps animation, costs speed and compatibility
Frames & Motion

How many previously decoded frames the motion search may predict from. More references help whenever the same content reappears - repetitive motion, cuts back to an earlier shot, animation that reuses cels - because the encoder can point at the frame that actually matches.

Cost is roughly linear in encoding time, and returns fall off quickly on ordinary live action past about five.

Hardware decoders limit this through the level: at 1080p, level 4.1 allows only four. Going higher produces a file that a compliant decoder is entitled to refuse.

3|The default, fine for general live action.
5|A good offline setting for detailed or repetitive material.
1|Fastest, and what some very limited decoders require.
16|The maximum; useful on animation, and out of spec for most hardware.
weightp
0-2 (default 2) - Weighted prediction for P-frames: 0 off, 1 weighted refs, 2 also duplicates; helps fades
Frames & Motion

Weighted prediction lets a P-frame scale and offset the reference it predicts from, so a frame that is simply brighter or darker than the one before does not have to be re-coded from scratch. Fades, flashes and lighting changes are where it earns its keep.

Mode 1 applies the weighting; mode 2 also allows duplicate weighted references, which helps most on fades. Both are essentially free.

Some older decoders and Blu-ray authoring require this off, and it is among the first tools dropped when decoder cost is the constraint. It is also incompatible with interlaced encoding, which x264 says outright.

2|The default; the strongest form, and what you want for fades.
1|Weighted references without duplicates, for stricter compatibility.
0|Off, for Blu-ray authoring or very old decoders.
direct
spatial, temporal, auto or none (default spatial) - How B-frames derive motion vectors they do not code
Frames & Motion

Direct mode lets a B-frame infer its motion vectors from neighbouring blocks instead of coding them, which is a large part of why B-frames are cheap. This chooses how that inference works: spatial predicts from neighbouring blocks in the same frame, temporal from the co-located block in a reference.

auto alternates between the two and picks whichever performed better, which costs a little analysis and is generally the best setting for offline encoding.

none disables direct mode entirely and forces every vector to be coded, which is a straightforward loss.

spatial|The default; predicts from spatial neighbours.
auto|Alternates and picks the better of the two; the best offline setting.
temporal|Predicts from the co-located block in a reference.
none|Disables direct mode; costs bitrate for no benefit.
me
dia, hex, umh, esa or tesa (default hex) - Integer pixel motion search; umh and up pay off on high-motion HD
Frames & Motion

The integer-pixel motion search pattern. dia checks a tiny diamond around the predicted vector, hex a hexagon, and umh runs an uneven multi-hexagon search that is far more likely to find large or unusual motion. esa and tesa search the whole merange exhaustively.

hex is the sensible default. umh is the one upgrade worth paying for, and it matters most at high resolution and on fast motion, where the right vector can be a long way from the prediction.

esa and tesa are exhaustive rather than clever: they cost enormously and almost never beat umh by enough to notice.

hex|The default, and a good speed to quality balance.
umh|High resolution or fast motion; the worthwhile upgrade.
dia|Fastest, for real-time encoding.
tesa|Exhaustive and extremely slow, for benchmarking rather than delivery.
subme
0-11 (default 7) - Subpixel motion estimation and mode decision quality; the main quality-versus-speed dial
Frames & Motion

Controls how hard the encoder refines a motion vector below whole-pixel precision, and how carefully it decides between modes. This is the single most effective quality-versus-speed dial x264 has.

The scale changes behaviour as it climbs: from 6 upward, rate-distortion optimisation is used for P and B frames, which is also the point at which psy-rd starts doing anything. From 8 upward, motion vectors and intra modes get an RD refinement pass.

10 and 11 additionally require trellis 2 and adaptive quantisation. Without both, x264 drops the setting back to 9 without saying so - so a subme of 10 typed on its own is a slower way of asking for 9.

Below 6 the encoder is making mode decisions on a rough estimate rather than on actual coding cost, which shows.

7|The default, and already past the point where psy-rd works.
10|Slow presets; RD refinement on vectors and intra modes, with trellis 2.
11|The maximum, for the last fraction of a percent.
2|Real-time encoding, where mode decisions have to be cheap.
merange
4-1024 (default 16) - Largest motion vector search range; only exceeds 16 with me umh, esa or tesa
Frames & Motion

The radius, in pixels, of the integer motion search. It bounds how far from the predicted position the encoder is willing to look for a match.

Raising it only does anything with a search pattern that can use the room: dia and hex have fixed shapes, and x264 clamps the range back to 16 for them, so this applies to umh, esa and tesa. With those, a larger range catches fast pans and whip motion at high resolution that would otherwise be coded as expensive intra blocks.

Cost grows quickly, and on ordinary content the extra range simply goes unused.

16|The default, enough for typical motion at up to 1080p.
24|Fast motion at 1080p and above, paired with me umh.
32|Whip pans and sports at 4K.
64|Rarely justified; the search cost is substantial.
partitions
p8x8, b8x8, i8x8, i4x4, p4x4, all or none (default varies by preset) - Which macroblock splits may be tried
Frames & Motion

H.264 can split a macroblock into smaller partitions so that motion is described at a finer scale. This lists which of those splits the encoder is allowed to consider, given as a comma-separated set.

Allowing more partitions lets the encoder describe complex motion and fine detail more accurately, at a cost in analysis time roughly proportional to how many it must test. Restricting them is a speed measure and shows up as blockier motion around detailed edges.

The preset already sets a sensible list - the medium preset uses p8x8, b8x8, i8x8 and i4x4 - so this is worth touching mainly to force all on a fast preset, or to cut the list on a slow one. Commas are the separator here and are safe; a colon would not be.

all|Every partition type; the most thorough analysis.
p8x8,b8x8,i8x8,i4x4|The set the medium and slower presets use.
i8x8,i4x4|Intra splits only, for a fast encode that still handles detail.
none|No sub-macroblock partitions; fastest and visibly blockier.
rc-lookahead
0-250 (default 40) - Frames looked ahead when deciding frame types and mb-tree; higher paces bits better
Frames & Motion

How many frames ahead the encoder looks before committing to a frame type and a quantiser. The lookahead drives both frame type decisions and mb-tree, which spends bits on blocks that later frames will keep referencing.

Longer lookahead paces bits better across a scene and makes mb-tree's estimates more useful, at the cost of memory and encoding latency. Past roughly the length of a typical shot there is nothing left to learn.

Setting it to 0 disables mb-tree outright - x264 says so and turns the flag off - which is why low-latency settings look worse at the same bitrate.

40|The default, a good match for most content.
60|Longer scenes and offline encoding, giving mb-tree more to work with.
0|Disables lookahead and mb-tree, for minimum latency.
250|The maximum; memory-hungry with little to show for it.
aq-mode
0-3 (default 1) - Adaptive quantisation: 0 off, 1 variance, 2 auto-variance, 3 with dark-scene bias
Quantization & Psychovisual

Adaptive quantisation moves bits between blocks within a frame, taking them from busy areas where quantisation error hides and giving them to flat ones where banding and blocking are obvious. Without it, dark and smooth regions are where an encode visibly falls apart first.

Mode 1 distributes by variance. Mode 2 adjusts the strength per frame using the frame's own content, which spreads bits more evenly across a varied sequence. Mode 3 adds a bias towards dark regions, which is where banding is most visible.

Turning it off raises PSNR and makes the result look worse, which is the whole reason metric-chasing settings do exactly that. It also has to be on for subme 10 and 11 to stay at the value you asked for.

1|The default variance-based distribution.
2|Auto-variance, adapting per frame; a good offline choice.
3|Auto-variance with a dark-scene bias, for night and shadow detail.
0|Off; higher metric scores, visibly worse picture.
aq-strength
0.0-3.0 (default 1.0) - Strength of adaptive quantisation; raise to cut blocking in flat areas, lower for grain
Quantization & Psychovisual

How far adaptive quantisation is allowed to shift the quantiser between blocks. Higher values take more bits out of detailed areas and put more into flat ones.

Raise it when flat regions - skies, walls, gradients, fades to black - show banding or blocking. Lower it when the source is grainy or heavily textured, because there the bits are better left where the detail is, and a strong setting will smooth the grain the rest of your settings are trying to keep.

The encoding preset does not touch this. Only x264's tunings move it, and none of those are in play here, so what you set is what runs.

1.0|The default, suitable for most live action.
0.6|Grainy or heavily textured sources, keeping bits on detail.
1.3|Flat, clean sources such as animation that band easily.
0.0|Disables the strength entirely, equivalent to turning AQ off.
psy-rd
rd,trellis - each 0.0-10.0 (default 1.0,0.0) - Keeps detail over PSNR; rd needs subme 6+, trellis needs trellis on
Quantization & Psychovisual

Psychovisual rate-distortion, given as two numbers. The first biases mode decisions towards keeping the same amount of visual energy as the source rather than towards the lowest measurable error, so the encoder stops preferring a smooth block over a detailed one that is slightly wrong. The second applies the same idea inside trellis quantisation.

This is what stops x264 output looking soft, and it is exactly why it costs PSNR and SSIM: it is deliberately choosing something those metrics score lower.

The first value needs subme 6 or higher to do anything, and the second needs trellis enabled. The psy row turns both off at once.

Write the pair separated by a comma. x264 documents it as rd:trellis, and a colon is what separates one parameter from the next in the string this grid builds, so a colon here gets the row refused.

1.0,0.0|The default; psy-rd on, psy-trellis off.
1.0,0.15|A mild trellis component, for detailed live action.
1.5,0.0|Stronger detail retention on grainy sources.
0.0,0.0|Off, for metric benchmarking only.
trellis
0-2 (default 1) - Trellis rate-distortion quantisation: 0 off, 1 on the final macroblock encode, 2 on all decisions
Quantization & Psychovisual

Trellis quantisation chooses which transform coefficients to keep by weighing what each one costs in bits against what it contributes, rather than rounding each in isolation. It recovers a useful amount of quality for the bitrate.

Mode 1 applies it only to the final encode of each macroblock. Mode 2 applies it during mode decision as well, so the choice between modes is made on the cost they will actually have - better, and slower.

subme 10 and 11 require mode 2 and silently fall back to 9 without it. Trellis also has to be on for the second half of psy-rd to do anything.

1|The default; trellis on the final macroblock encode.
2|On all mode decisions; the offline choice and required by subme 10+.
0|Off, for real-time encoding.
chroma-qp-offset
-12 to 12 (default 0, plus x264's own -2 while psy is on) - Shifts the chroma quantiser relative to luma
Quantization & Psychovisual

Offsets the quantiser used for the chroma planes from the one used for luma. Negative values quantise chroma more finely, spending more bits on colour; positive values coarsen it to spend more on brightness detail.

The parameter's own default is 0, but x264 adds -2 of its own whenever psy is enabled, which is why a stream encoded at the defaults reports a chroma offset of -2. What you type here is added to that, so -4 comes out as -6 in the stream and lands at the same place a -4 in the encoder would.

Negative values are worth trying on saturated, colour-critical material, and on animation where flat colour areas show chroma banding. Positive values are a way to buy luma detail on a tight bitrate.

0|The default, leaving x264's own psy offset in place.
-2|Extra bits on colour; useful for animation and saturated sources.
-4|A strong chroma bias, for colour-critical work.
2|Coarser chroma, buying luma detail at low bitrates.
dct-decimate
0 or 1 (default 1) - Discards near-empty blocks of coefficients; turn off to keep faint grain and texture
Quantization & Psychovisual

DCT decimation throws away a coded block whose transform coefficients are few enough and small enough that x264 judges it to be carrying nothing worth the bits. On most material that is free bitrate: the block was noise.

On grainy or lightly textured sources it is not free, because the blocks being dropped are the grain. Turning it off is one of the standard grain-retention measures, alongside a negative deblock and a raised psy-rd, and it costs bitrate in exactly the way keeping grain always does.

It matters on very clean synthetic content too - gradients, fog, soft animation backgrounds - where the discarded block was a subtle shade change rather than nothing, and dropping it is what banding looks like from the inside.

1|The default; near-empty blocks discarded.
0|Keeps them, for grain retention and smooth gradients.
nr
0-65536 (default 0, off) - In-encoder noise reduction; removes fine noise before it is coded, at a cost in detail
Quantization & Psychovisual

Applies noise reduction inside the encoder, removing low-amplitude detail before it is coded. Noise is close to random and therefore expensive, so removing it can save a substantial amount of bitrate on a noisy source.

The cost is that it cannot distinguish sensor noise from fine texture, so it removes both. Values are on a wide scale and the effect climbs quickly; a few hundred is a mild clean-up, several thousand is visibly smoothing. Anything above 65536 is clamped back to it.

For film grain you almost always want to keep, prefer psy-rd, dct-decimate 0 and a negative deblock over this.

0|The default; no noise reduction.
100|A mild clean-up for lightly noisy digital footage.
500|Noticeable smoothing, saving real bitrate on noisy sources.
1000|Strong; removes fine texture along with the noise.
qcomp
0.0-1.0 (default 0.60) - QP curve compression; 0.0 acts like constant bitrate, 1.0 like constant QP
Quantization & Psychovisual

Compresses the curve that maps frame complexity to quantiser, deciding how bitrate is shared between easy and hard scenes. At 0.0 every frame is pushed to the same size, which is constant bitrate behaviour and makes complex scenes fall apart. At 1.0 every frame gets the same quantiser, which is constant quality and lets file size follow the content.

The default sits between the two, giving hard scenes more bits than constant quality would while still holding overall size near the target.

It interacts with mb-tree, which uses this value in its own calculations, so large changes affect more than the scene-to-scene split. A value of exactly 1.0 turns mb-tree off altogether, there being no curve left for it to shape.

0.60|The default, a sound balance for VBR.
0.75|Closer to constant quality; better on content with a wide difficulty range.
0.50|Tighter size control, at the cost of the hardest scenes.
1.00|Constant quantiser behaviour, and mb-tree off with it.
mbtree
0 or 1 (default 1) - Macroblock tree rate control; spends bits on the blocks later frames keep referencing
Rate Control

Macroblock tree looks over the lookahead window and works out, block by block, how much of what comes later depends on each one. A block that later frames keep predicting from gets a lower quantiser, because the bits spent there are reused many times over; a block nothing refers to again gets a higher one.

It is one of the largest single quality-per-bit wins x264 has on ordinary content, which is why it is on by default. Turning it off is for material where the estimate misleads, or where bitrate has to stay predictable frame by frame.

Two other settings switch it off without being asked: an rc-lookahead of 0, since there is nothing left to look at, and a qcomp of 1.0. It also overrides pbratio outright, which is why that parameter does nothing at all until this is off.

1|The default; mb-tree on.
0|Off, handing B-frame weighting back to pbratio.
vbv-maxrate
kbit/s (default 0, off) - Ceiling on local bitrate; set with vbv-bufsize for streaming or hardware decoders
Rate Control

Caps the bitrate over any window the buffer covers, rather than over the file as a whole. Without it, a constant-quality encode is free to spend whatever a difficult scene needs, which is fine for a local file and fatal for a stream or a hardware decoder with a fixed input rate.

It only takes effect alongside vbv-bufsize; a maxrate with no buffer size does nothing, and x264 says so and ignores it.

Constraining the rate necessarily costs quality exactly where the content is hardest, so set it to what the target actually requires and no lower.

6000|Roughly a 1080p streaming ceiling.
3000|A conservative cap for constrained connections.
40000|Blu-ray's video ceiling.
0|The default; no cap.
vbv-bufsize
kbit (default 0, off) - Size of the VBV buffer; smaller windows hold the maxrate ceiling more tightly
Rate Control

The size of the notional buffer the maxrate is enforced over, in kilobits. Together the two say how much the bitrate may vary and over what period.

A buffer equal to the maxrate allows one second of variation, which is the usual streaming arrangement. Smaller buffers hold the ceiling more tightly and hurt quality on hard scenes; larger ones let the encoder spend where it needs to at the cost of a longer startup delay and more risk of underrun.

Like maxrate, this does nothing on its own, and x264 says so.

6000|One second of buffer against a 6000 kbit/s ceiling.
12000|Two seconds; gentler on difficult scenes, slower to start.
30000|Blu-ray's buffer size.
0|The default; no buffer constraint.
qpmin
0-69 (default 0) - The best quantiser rate control may use; raise it to stop easy scenes soaking up bitrate
Rate Control

A floor on the quantiser, which is a ceiling on how many bits any one frame may be given. Lower quantisers mean higher quality, so this bounds how good the encode is allowed to get.

Raising it stops easy scenes being encoded at a quality nobody will notice. In a bitrate-targeted or filesize-targeted encode that frees bits for the difficult material; in CRF it simply caps quality on the easy parts and shrinks the file.

Values above about 10 start to be visible on flat content, so this is a fine adjustment rather than a blunt one. Anything above 69 is clamped back to it.

0|The default; no floor.
10|Stops easy scenes spending more than they need.
15|A firmer cap, noticeably smaller files on easy content.
qpmax
0-69 (default 69) - The worst quantiser rate control may use; lower it to stop hard scenes collapsing
Rate Control

A ceiling on the quantiser, bounding how far quality is allowed to fall when the rate controller runs short of bits.

Lowering it prevents the blocky collapse that difficult scenes show at constrained bitrates. The consequence is that the encoder can no longer hit its bitrate target on those scenes and will overshoot instead - a quality floor and a size target cannot both be guaranteed.

The default of 69 is the highest quantiser x264 has, which is effectively no limit, so this only matters in bitrate-targeted or filesize-targeted encoding where the target is tight. A larger number is clamped back to 69 rather than refused.

69|The default; effectively unlimited.
40|Prevents the worst collapse on hard scenes.
35|A firm quality floor, at the cost of size predictability.
qpstep
0-69 (default 4) - The largest quantiser change allowed between consecutive frames
Rate Control

Limits how far the quantiser may move from one frame to the next. It exists to stop the rate controller reacting so sharply to a change in difficulty that quality visibly pulses.

Raising it lets rate control respond faster to a sudden change in scene complexity, which helps it hold a bitrate target through hard cuts, at the risk of visible quality steps.

Lowering it makes quality smoother over time and leaves the controller slower to react, which can overshoot the target when a difficult scene arrives abruptly.

4|The default.
2|Smoother quality over time; slower to react to scene changes.
8|Faster reaction, better target tracking, more visible steps.
ipratio
Float, normally above 1.0 (default 1.40) - How much finer I-frames are quantised than P-frames
Rate Control

The quantiser ratio between I-frames and P-frames. I-frames are coded without reference to anything else and everything after them predicts from them, so spending extra bits there pays off across the whole GOP.

Raising it gives keyframes more bits, which helps when scene changes look soft for a moment before recovering. Lowering it evens the frames out, which can reduce the visible pulse some content shows at each keyframe.

x264 does not bound this, so a value below 1.0 is accepted and means keyframes coded worse than the frames predicting from them - which is not something to ask for. Changes here interact with qcomp, since both shape how bits are distributed across frame types.

1.40|The default.
1.30|Flatter distribution; less visible pulsing at keyframes.
1.50|More bits on keyframes, sharpening scene starts.
pbratio
Float, normally above 1.0 (default 1.30) - How much coarser B-frames are quantised; needs mbtree 0 to do anything
Rate Control

The quantiser ratio between P-frames and B-frames. B-frames are usually not referenced by anything, so quantising them more coarsely is nearly free - the error does not propagate.

Raising it takes more bits out of B-frames and gives them to the P-frames that everything predicts from. Lowering it evens the two out, which is worth doing when b-pyramid is on, because then some B-frames are references and their errors do propagate.

Mb-tree is on by default and overrides this completely - it is deciding the same thing per block, with better information. Until mbtree is set to 0 this parameter is accepted and does nothing, and the encoded stream does not even list it.

1.30|The default.
1.20|Evens out B-frames; sensible with b-pyramid enabled.
1.40|More bits diverted to P-frames.
crf-max
0.0-51.0 (default off) - With CRF and VBV together, the worst rate factor the encoder may fall back to
Rate Control

When CRF is combined with a VBV constraint, the encoder will raise its rate factor - lowering quality - as far as it needs to in order to respect the bitrate ceiling. This caps how far it may go.

Reaching that cap means the encoder can no longer satisfy VBV, so it will exceed the ceiling rather than degrade further. That is the trade: a guaranteed minimum quality in exchange for a bitrate that may breach the constraint on the hardest material.

It does nothing without vbv-maxrate and vbv-bufsize set, and nothing outside CRF mode.
